extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide for journalists that gives inclusive-language recommendations, capitalization and hyphenation rules, preferred and disfavored terms, and usage notes for reporting on identity, religion, health and culture. It is meant to guide word choice, attribution and sensitivity in news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBTQ+ terminology and community
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylebook notes: "It may be tempting for journalists to refer to the LGBTQ+ community. In reality, it is a broad and sometimes loosely bound group of communities comprising people from all races, religions, cultures and walks of life. Referring to LGBTQ+ people is usually more accurate than defining it as one community." The Diversity Style Guide recommends the more inclusive term LGBTQ+. Do not refer to an individual as LGBTQ or LGBTQ+. Updated March 2023
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LGBTQ+ (recommended) but avoid calling an individual "LGBTQ" or "LGBTQ+." Prefer "LGBTQ+ people" over lumping everyone into a single "community."

rubrics_metrics.name: lifestyle (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inaccurate term sometimes used to describe the lives of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people. Sexual orientation may be part of a broader lifestyle but is not one in itself, just as there is no “straight” lifestyle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using "lifestyle" to describe sexual orientation. See sexual orientation, sexual preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: linguistic racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic racism is discrimination based on accent, dialect or speech patterns. Acts of linguistic racism can be overt or covert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples (mocking the way someone speaks; telling someone they're unintelligible because of an accent; complimenting someone for speaking English well even if born speaking it). Note that certain languages and dialects (Spanish, Asian languages, African American Vernacular English) may be undervalued, and cite common microaggressive comments like “Where are you from?” and “You speak English well for someone who looks like you.” Added June 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: little person
rubrics_metrics.description: See dwarf, midget, short stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to related entries (dwarf, short stature) for preferred usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: liturgy capitalization and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Has two sets of meanings, one for Western Christians and the other for Eastern Christians. Among Roman Catholics and Protestants, lowercase liturgy means a standard set of prayers and practices for public worship. It can also be used as a synonym for the service of worship in churches that use such forms – most commonly the Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran. With reference to Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics, uppercase Liturgy; avoid the lowercase use of the word with their churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase "liturgy" for Western Christian contexts; capitalize "Liturgy" for Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics. Note that nonliturgical churches (e.g., many Baptist, Pentecostal) vary services weekly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lord (capitalize for monotheistic God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize when referring to God in a monotheistic faith, as in Lord Jesus or in Lord Krishna.

rubrics_metrics.name: lover (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term preferred by some individuals for a gay, lesbian, bisexual or heterosexual person’s sexual partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives include girlfriend, boyfriend and partner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubavitch/Lubavitcher (use and background)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the largest branches of Hasidic Judaism, originated in Russia in the 18th century; also called Chabad-Lubavitch. Some groups regard Schneerson as the Messiah and await his return; others do not. The branch is called Chabad-Lubavitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lubavitch/Lubavitcher as appropriate; see Chabad for related usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: lupus (health reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronic disease that affects immunity. Normally, the body's immune system makes proteins called antibodies to protect against viruses, bacteria and other foreign materials. Lupus causes the immune system to attack healthy tissues and organs. It can harm various parts of the body, especially the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, brain and heart. Lupus most often affects black women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lutheran (denomination usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of a Protestant denomination that traces its roots to Martin Luther. The two major Lutheran bodies in the U.S. are the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA on second reference) and the smaller Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod (Missouri Synod on second reference). Missouri Synod churches are far more theologically conservative than ELCA churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On first reference, use "the Rev." and the cleric’s full name. On second reference use only the cleric’s last name. Use "pastor" if a minister leads a congregation. Note differences among branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: madman (avoid/see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See crazy/crazed, psycho, nuts, lunatic, deranged, wacko.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pejorative terms; use recommended entries for mental health terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: madrassa
rubrics_metrics.description: A Muslim place of learning usually associated with a mosque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mahatma (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanskrit term for "great soul." Became the honorific for M.K. Gandhi during India's struggle for independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: mainline Protestant (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A designation for a group of moderate-to-liberal Protestant churches. The most prominent are United Methodist Church, ELCA, Presbyterian Church (USA), Episcopal Church, United Church of Christ, Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), and American Baptist Churches in the U.S.A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaysian names (naming rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Malaysians do not use family names, but, as in Burma, use honorifics. Malaysian Chinese and Malaysian Muslims follow special naming rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware naming conventions and consult appropriate guidance for second references.

rubrics_metrics.name: male-to-female (MtF), female-to-male (FtM) (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: These terms used to be a common way to describe a trans person. In recent years, they’ve come to be considered outdated and sometimes offensive descriptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid MtF/FtM except when quoting; instead use trans woman, trans man. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandarin (language caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: important differences from Cantonese. The official language of China and Taiwan, derived from different dialects but not itself a dialect. The term Mandarin refers to the spoken language. One speaks Mandarin but writes Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that China has one written language using characters understood by literate people, but many spoken regional dialects (Shanghainese, Fukienese) are unintelligible across regions. Distinguish Mandarin from Cantonese in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: manga (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A type of comic that developed in Japan. Manga have evolved stylistically and become popular worldwide; many characters have large eyes. With complex story lines and some adult content, manga have a broad appeal among children, teens and adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: manong/manang (terms of respect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manong is a term of respect that precedes the first name of older Filipino men; manang for older Filipina women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as cultural honorifics where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: mantra (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllable, word or phrase with spiritual power, chanted or held in the mind in meditation or ritual. Common among Hindus, Buddhists and Jains and traditionally drawn from Sanskrit scriptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounce and contextualize appropriately; do not conflate with secular phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: marriage (same-sex reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: In June 2015, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Obergefell v. Hodges that every American has the constitutional right to marry the person they love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred terminology includes "marriage equality" and "marriage for same-sex couples." Avoid "gay marriage" and "same-sex marriage" as they can suggest difference from other marriages.

rubrics_metrics.name: martial arts (usage caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Armed and unarmed fighting sports or skills, mainly of East Asian origin. Unarmed forms emphasize striking or grappling. Many forms influenced by Taoism and Buddhism. Examples: kung fu, judo, karate, kendo. Derivatives seen in parkour and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: martial-arts imagery can be abused (e.g., editorial cartoons). See Asia, use and abuse of images; Buddhism; stereotypes; Taoism.

rubrics_metrics.name: masjid
rubrics_metrics.description: Urdu word for mosque, a place of prayer and meeting for Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use masjid when culturally or linguistically appropriate; note historical/political relevance where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: mass (Catholic usage and capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used by Latin Catholics and some high-church Anglicans for a worship service that includes the celebration of Holy Communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term cannot be used for services that do not include Communion. Capitalize when referring to the celebration of worship in the Roman Catholic Church. Lowercase any preceding adjectives (e.g., funeral Mass). The Associated Press accepts only "celebrated" (not "said"). Orthodox Christians call their Eucharistic service the Divine Liturgy.

rubrics_metrics.name: mass incarceration (definition and context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass incarceration is increased rates of imprisonment resulting from tougher penalties, especially for drug offenses. Arrests and mandatory minimum sentences have fueled this since the 1970s; African Americans have been locked up in disproportionate numbers; sentences are longer for Black men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context and cite sources (ACLU, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Southern Coalition for Social Justice). Note increases in women incarcerated and racial disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: master bedroom/bathroom (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used to denote the largest bedrooms/bathrooms; have racist and sexist undertones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid "master bedroom/bathroom." Use alternatives like "owner’s suite" and "primary bedroom."

rubrics_metrics.name: McCarran-Walter Act (historical context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officially the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952; allowed Asians to apply for citizenship but set immigration quotas from each Asian country at only 100 annually. Liberalization in 1965 allowed larger-scale migration of Asians to the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: mehndi (definition and cultural use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Indian and diaspora art of intricate hand/body decoration using henna dye; used mainly by brides in marriage ceremonies but now popular as an exotic decoration and non-permanent "tattoo."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize cultural significance and avoid exoticizing; note pop-culture usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: MENA (Middle Eastern or North African) abbreviation use
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Middle East and North Africa. People of MENA descent can mark "White, including Middle Eastern" or "some other race" on Census forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "Middle Eastern or North African descent" on first reference. If you use the MENA abbreviation, explain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: mental health (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of well-being in which someone can cope with common stresses and live and work productively to his or her full potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cultural differences, subjective assessments and competing professional theories that affect definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: mental health professional (identification guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many types of professionals may work with individuals experiencing mental health challenges: psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists, social workers, marriage and family therapists, etc. HIPAA may limit information a professional can legally share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the professional how he or she should be identified, based on formal training. Provide broad definitions (psychiatrist: can prescribe psychotropic meds; psychoanalyst: specific training in unconscious; psychologist: trained in psychology, testing; psychotherapist: umbrella term). Avoid using "shrink" except in a quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: mental illness, mental health disorder (people-first language)
rubrics_metrics.description: A health condition that changes a person’s thinking, feelings or behavior and that causes distress and difficulty functioning. Covers wide range of conditions; severity varies. One in four adults experiences mental illness in a given year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language ("she experiences symptoms of psychosis" vs "she is psychotic"). Refer to an individual’s mental illness only when relevant and when diagnosis comes from a proper source. Specify the specific illness when possible. Use quotes when officials or family use blanket terms and indicate when diagnosis is unconfirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: mentally retarded, mentally disabled, intellectually disabled, developmentally disabled (terminology guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like mentally retarded, retard and mental retardation were once common but are now considered outdated and offensive. Rosa’s Law (2010) replaced "mental retardation" with "intellectual disability" in many government contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always try to specify type of disability. Use people-first language ("people with mental disabilities" rather than "the mentally disabled"). Outdated terms may be appropriate in historical contexts if attributed or noted as historical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: messiah, Messiah (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hebrew term meaning "the anointed one." For Christians, the one and only Messiah is Jesus Christ. Jews await the coming of the Messiah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize in religious uses and lowercase in secular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodist Episcopal Church (historical note)
rubrics_metrics.description: American Protestant denomination whose initial progress in ministering to black Americans was thwarted by segregationist policies. Term Methodist originated as a nickname for 18th-century Oxford students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mexican vs Mexican-American (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use "Mexican" when referring to anyone of Mexican citizenship, and use "Mexican American" when referring to those of Mexican ancestry who are permanent residents or citizens of the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: microaggressions, racial microaggressions (definition and impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slights and snubs based on racial discrimination, some unintentional. Can be questions, expressions, or behaviors regarding identity or abilities. Examples include "You don’t act like a normal Black person," or locking the car door when someone perceived as a threat walks by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note accumulating mental-health and performance effects; refer to scholarship (Derald Wing Sue) and projects (Seattle Times "Under Our Skin").

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle East (terminology and geography)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcontinental region centered on Western Asia, Southeastern Europe and Northern Africa. The AP says it applies to southwest Asia west of Pakistan and Afghanistan and northeastern Africa (Egypt, Sudan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Middle East" is preferred; "Mideast" is also acceptable. Corresponding adjective is "Middle-Eastern" and the derived noun is "Middle-Easterner."

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle Passage (historical term)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transatlantic voyages between Africa and the Americas that claimed approximately 1.8 million African slaves over about 350 years; some 12 million slaves were packed into ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See slavery entry for more context.

rubrics_metrics.name: midget (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See dwarf, little person, short stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid usage; consult related entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: midlife (preferred term)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to people in midlife are more inclusive than using boomer(s). Midlife generally identifies years between early 40s and early 60s, though precision is slippery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer "midlife" over birth-cohort labels. Be aware historical definitions varied (middle age as early 35).

rubrics_metrics.name: militant (usage cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used to describe an aggressive activist or someone engaged in warfare; a militant view can be extremist. Militant is neutral; terrorist indicates reprehensible behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use "militant" in place of "terrorist." Avoid using "militant" to describe a Black person who is simply hostile, belligerent or controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Million Man March (event)
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington rally held on Oct. 16, 1995, organized by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan and the Rev. Benjamin Chavis to draw attention to social conditions of black men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note differing crowd estimates and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Million Woman March (event)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philadelphia march and rally held on Oct. 25, 1997, organized by community activists Asia Coney and Phile Chionesu seeking to build coalitions within the black community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note estimated attendance and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: minister (title usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Protestant denominations use "minister" to describe clergy, but it is not a formal title and is not capitalized. In Catholicism, a distinction exists between ordained ministers (priests and deacons) and lay ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nation of Islam uses "Minister" as a title and it should be capitalized before the person’s name. Use appropriate capitalization and title conventions for the faith tradition in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: minority, racial minority (avoid as label for individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically referred to non-White racial groups, indicating numerical smaller size. Defining people of color as "minorities" is not recommended because of changing demographics and reinforcement of inferiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid referring to an individual as a "minority." Use self-identification or specific terms. The term may be needed in contexts ("minority contracting") that reflect data collected with those categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: misgender (definition and breaking news practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of referring to someone by the wrong gender (using incorrect pronouns or gender-specific words not conforming to the person's gender identity/expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some media adopt avoiding pronouns and gender-specific words in breaking news coverage when a person's gender can't be confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: mixed-status couple/family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually refers to couples or families with members who have different immigration status (e.g., one undocumented parent, one legal resident parent, a U.S.-born citizen child).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware the term is also used in health contexts to describe serodiscordant sexual relationships (HIV+ and HIV- partners). Clarify meaning in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: mixed, mixed-race (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See biracial, multiracial, mixed-race, two or more races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preferred contemporary terms (biracial/multiracial) and follow related entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: model minority (definition and critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that a particular ethnic, racial or religious group achieves greater success than the population average; in the U.S. most often refers to Asians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: the myth implies group-based advantage, ignores discrimination history, masks socioeconomic diversity, and stigmatizes group members who do not meet expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern Orthodox (definition and nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement within Orthodox Judaism that tends to integrate traditional practices with secular life while retaining Jewish identity. Modern Orthodox adherents may keep kosher, observe Sabbath, and often wear a yarmulke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is accepted among Jews but encompasses a wide spectrum; clarify with subjects where they see themselves within Modern Orthodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mongolian names (naming rules caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely complex naming rules involving patronymics, matronymics and clan names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware second reference and consult appropriate conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mongoloid (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used in the late 19th century to refer to people who had Down syndrome; considered highly derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always avoid use of "mongoloid" to refer to someone with Down syndrome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Montgomery bus boycott (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yearlong protest in Montgomery that galvanized the civil-rights movement and led to the 1956 Supreme Court decision declaring segregated seating on buses unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See civil rights movement entry for broader context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moonie (derogatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory term for a member of the Unification Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should not use it except in direct quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mormon Church (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proper name of the church rather than slang or shortened forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moslem (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: An outdated term for Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should not be used unless part of a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motown (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly black-owned record company that became culturally influential in the 1960s; Motown Records is now part of Universal Music Group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be used as adjective to describe the musical style or the city (Detroit) where it originated.

rubrics_metrics.name: MSM (definition, public-health context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for "men who have sex with men." It is a behavioral and public-health category, used in medical or scientific contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not reference sexual identity and is not synonymous with gay and bisexual men. See down low.

rubrics_metrics.name: mulatto (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has a white parent and a black parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the term; considered insensitive. Use "biracial." See biracial.

rubrics_metrics.name: mullah (title usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Shiite term for lower-level clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the title when it precedes a name.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiple personality disorder (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See dissociative identity disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use current diagnostic terminology (dissociative identity disorder) rather than outdated names.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiple sclerosis (MS) (health reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information within the brain and between the brain and body; symptoms vary widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to describe a person as "someone with multiple sclerosis," followed by short explanation. Avoid saying a person "suffers from" or "is afflicted with" the disease. "MS" is acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumbai (current place name)
rubrics_metrics.description: The current term for the Indian city previously known as Bombay. Renaming of Indian cities began after 1947 and continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use current local names (Mumbai) instead of colonial-era names (Bombay) unless historical context warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: murti (religious image usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced "MOOR-tee." In Hinduism, an image or icon of God used during worship. A manifestation, embodiment or personification of the divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the word "idol" as a synonym.

rubrics_metrics.name: muscular dystrophy (health reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Could refer to any of more than 30 genetic diseases characterized by progressive weakness and degeneration of muscles controlling movement. Onset varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe a person as "someone with muscular dystrophy" followed by a short explanation. Avoid "suffers from" or "is afflicted with." "MD" acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muslim American (hyphenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hyphenate. Use hyphen when the term is a compound modifier (e.g., Muslim-American community).

rubrics_metrics.name: Muslim, Muslims (noun vs adjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Muslim is a follower of Muhammad and tenets of Islam. The word Muslim is a noun; use the adjective Islamic when referring to the faith or Islamic world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mx. (gender-neutral title)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced "mix," Mx. is a gender-neutral courtesy title preferred by some transgender or nonbinary people who do not identify as male or female and so do not want to use "Mr." or "Ms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mx. when a person prefers it. Note its rising use in major news organizations (example: The New York Times first used it in 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myanmar (pronunciation and see)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced MEE-YAHN-mar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Burma entry for related context.

rubrics_metrics.name: NAACP (acronym usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded Feb. 12, 1909 by a multiracial group of activists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acronym is acceptable in all references. Use "Legal Defense Fund" on second reference for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: nation (federally recognized tribes as nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federally recognized tribes are considered self-governing – or sovereign nations – by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See American Indian, Native American, tribe entries for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation of Islam (usage and follower terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: A religious and political organization formed in 1930 by Wallace Fard Muhammad with aims around improving conditions of Black people; tenets differ from traditional Islam. Followers should be referred to as members of the Nation of Islam. The term Black Muslim, once associated, is now considered derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "members of the Nation of Islam." Nation of Islam clergymen use the title minister, which should be capitalized on first reference before a name; on second reference use only the person's last name.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Negro League (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional baseball league for blacks founded in 1920 by Andrew Rube Foster. Major League Baseball excluded blacks during Jim Crow so black teams formed their own leagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical context and note integration (Jackie Robinson in 1947) and later decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native American, Native (usage and specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Native American and American Indian are both generally acceptable and can be used interchangeably, although individuals may have a preference. "Native American" expanded in the 1960s. Use Native American and American Indian interchangeably but the term is used only to describe groups of Native Americans (two or more individuals of different tribal affiliation). Journalists should always identify people by their preferred tribal affiliation when reporting on individuals or tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "native-born" to describe someone born in the U.S. but not American Indian. Note federal recognition and tribal enrollment rules. 2016 legislation replaced the term American Indian with Native American in federal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known as Kanaka Maoli in Hawaiian; Native Hawaiians trace lineage and language to Polynesians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander (Census definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander as "a person having origins in any of the original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, or other Pacific Islands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The racial categories reflect a social definition of race, not biological or anthropological definitions; they may include national origin or sociocultural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (umbrella term)
rubrics_metrics.description: This umbrella term, used by the U.S. Census Bureau and other agencies, includes people who can trace their roots to the original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa or other Pacific Islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro (avoid; exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use African American or black. Do not use to describe a person of African descent. Term acceptable in organization names and historical references (e.g., National Council of Negro Women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid "Negro" in contemporary reporting; it's out of date and potentially offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro Codes (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See Black codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro National Anthem (historical/cultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Began as the 1899 poem "Lift Ev’ry Voice and Sing" by James Weldon Johnson, set to music by his brother; adopted by NAACP as its official song and represents resilience and strength of Black people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context and may include audio resources when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: neo-paganism (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to describe contemporary paganism, as opposed to ancient paganism; some prefer "pagan," others "neo-pagan."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how groups self-identify and avoid conflating diverse practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nepali (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: People from Nepal are known variously as Nepalese or Nepali, the latter favored in current usage though U.S. press uses Nepalese when referring to those in the United States. "Nepali" can be both noun and adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate demonym depending on context (Nepali favored) and note distinctions for U.S. usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: neuroatypical, neurodivergent (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used to describe people of atypical developmental, intellectual and cognitive abilities (e.g., autism or another developmental difference). People not on the autism spectrum may be called neurotypical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these terms respectfully to describe neurodiversity; follow individuals' self-identification where possible.
